spec.title: Precompute offline, serve instantly
spec.description: The batch pipeline has no latency budget and does all the heavy computation. The serving path reads a precomputed answer. Neither constrains the other — which is the entire reason to separate them.

groups.label: Batch — runs on a schedule, may fail and retry

steps.text: Mappers read partitions of the raw log in parallel and emit key-value pairs — say (category, sale_amount). Each mapper is independent, so this scales by adding machines.

The shuffle groups every pair by key and routes each key to one reducer. This is the expensive step: it moves data across the network, and a single hot key sends everything to one reducer — the same skew problem as a hot shard.
Each reducer sees all values for its keys and aggregates them — summing, ranking, counting distinct.

Output is written as a complete new result set and swapped in atomically, rather than mutated in place. A failed job leaves the previous results serving, which is why batch failures are invisible to users.
The user request never triggers computation. It reads a value that was calculated hours ago.
Which is why this is fast and cheap: the hard work happened once, offline, for all users — instead of once per request.

Batch wins when the answer tolerates being hours old, the computation needs a global view (ranking requires seeing everything), and reprocessing matters — a ranking bug is fixed by rerunning over retained raw events.

The failure mode to watch is a silently stale result set: the job fails repeatedly while serving looks perfectly healthy. Monitor result age, not just job success — the same trap as a stale autocomplete trie.
Streaming is the answer when freshness is the requirement. Many systems run both — a batch layer for correctness and completeness, a streaming layer for recency — and merge at read time.
